videos.title: Why count++ lies: a read, an add and a write, lost deposits on a thread-safe map, and a payment recorded twice
Ana and Ben pay each other at the same moment: two keys taken in opposite orders freeze for good, one lock order breaks the circle, and a lock that gives up needs a random rest
Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register
Only the same lock or the same volatile field links two threads: a reader that locks its own object never sees the balance
The thrifty manager: seven orders through the four rules show a pool queues first and grows second, so an endless rail keeps the maximum of 64 from ever calling a cook
Four waiters and a board of order slips: a virtual thread is put down at every blocking call with its frames on the heap, and any free carrier picks it up again
Two cooks, one ticket: the bell wakes both, so a woken cook checks the rail again in a while loop, and with two kinds of sleepers on one bench notify() can stall the kitchen
It says 41, please make it 42: compare-and-set writes only if nobody beat you to it, the loser reads again and retries, the update function can run twice, and the check belongs inside the request
The ticket for table 4: thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens a ticket for a ticket, thenCombine waits for two, and the calls must start first (347 ms side by side, 661 ms chained)
A hot pan a waiter can't put down: on JDK 21 to 23 a virtual thread holding a synchronized monitor pins its carrier (a 343 ms gap, 3 pins), a ReentrantLock unmounts, and JDK 24 cooled the pan

Four cooks, one pile: each cook splits onto his own stack, an idle cook steals the biggest bundle from the bottom, fork, compute, join keeps four leaves running (the wrong order runs one), and a cook on the phone stalls the shared common pool
Handing an object to another thread is a write: a reader can find the rate card before its fields, unless a seal such as volatile or final fields stops it
Three rules before any code: a bank that makes and loses money without an error, a surprise auditor who can look at any moment, and the ledger those rules design
A thread's six states as places on a map, the call behind each move, and interrupt as a note the thread must notice and put back
Chopping cooks and oven cooks: checksums stop getting faster at one thread per core, a page that waits 180 of 200 ms needs ten threads per core, and 400 requests a second for 250 ms keep 100 inside
volatile keeps every read fresh and every write visible, yet two threads still read 41 and both write 42: the fix is one atomic step
A head waiter who calls the helpers back: a scope forks, fails fast so join throws at about 100 ms, and close waits for every subtask; a scoped value is a note pinned to the order

A cleaner by the clock or one who rests after each round: after one 250 ms run, fixed rate runs the overdue rounds back to back, fixed delay shifts every later one, and a run that throws ends the schedule without a word
A latch opens for good at zero, a barrier lets a full group through and closes again, and a semaphore hands out permits anyone can give back
A bounded queue makes the fast producer wait, and one poison pill per consumer, put after the last producer, stops every writer cleanly
One key for the vault: a checker that skips the key sees money in flight, the holder can walk back in, a private key nobody can borrow, and no slow calls while you hold it
get then put leaves a gap where a second thread reads the old total; merge reads, adds and writes under one bin lock, while writes to other bins run in parallel
Every table keeps its own waiter: a 200 ms checkout waits 195 ms but holds its thread, so 200 threads stop at 1,000 a second on a bored machine, and a slow bank cuts that to 156

The vault with controls on the door: tryLock gives up after 200 ms, lockInterruptibly hears the shutdown, unlock goes in finally, each Condition is its own bench, and a reader who asks for the write lock waits for itself
A race needs state that is shared and changing: take away either one, and there is nothing to lock

Ticket 42: a time limit ends the wait, not the work, and cancel(true) only leaves a note, so the cook at the oven stops, the cook who looks up stops, the one who never looks runs on, and every ticket says cancelled at once

When the steak burns: the note skips every station until the pass, arrives in an envelope, a kitchen timer frees the manager but not the cook, and each supplier call must be unable to fail before allOf
Checking twice without volatile: the lock-free fast path can hand out a table that isn't null and is still empty, until volatile hangs the OPEN sign last
A 20-pan grill and a hook of 20 tokens: a pool of 20 virtual threads makes the whole order wait (3,628 ms), one shared Semaphore(20) around the save alone does not (604 ms)

A manager who hires a cook for every order: a new thread per tiny task costs more than the task and has no ceiling, a pool hires its cooks once, shutdown only locks the door, and awaitTermination waits

A stuck Saturday night: name tags on the cooks, a note left on the waiter's jacket, the board by the pass (2 active, 4 queued, 4 rejected), cooks waiting for tickets behind them, and closing the kitchen in order
A thread is a clerk with its own notepad (the stack) and a shared filing cabinet (the heap); run() is a plain call, start() makes a thread, join() waits for it
Four access modes as a ladder of parcel labels: each adds one promise, and release/acquire is weaker than volatile, not just cheaper

Two test threads that never overlap catch nothing: a start latch, more threads than cores and many rounds make them collide, a latch with a deadline replaces the sleep, and jcstress counts every outcome

Ten waiters quietly protected ten burners: a fixed pool of 10 also kept the database to 10 callers, a plain swap fails 237 of 300 requests, a Semaphore(10) writes the limit back, and Little's law shows where requests wait

Locked reads one account at a time are a panorama, and the sum tears; a snapshot takes every lock in id order, copies into a record that never changes, and publishes it with one volatile write, so readers see old or new, never a mix

One request, every limit written down: its own virtual thread, 20 grill tokens for the safety service, the 8 + 80 ledger pool, and one 300 ms deadline that interrupts the call and lets small amounts through
